rules.typing_s: max(10 s, chars / 200 chars-per-minute); interrupt = 2 s; images not counted.
rules.read_s: words of the latest assistant message (by message.id) containing text that finished before the input, / 250 wpm, capped at 10 min; each assistant message is credited to at most one human input (no double counting); for the AskUserQuestion answer, the words of the question and options.
rules.active_s_paste_adjusted: same, but likely-pasted inputs (over 2000 chars, plus two shorter ones that are a template and pasted terminal output) have typing capped at 3 min
rules.engagement_sessions: runs of inputs with gaps < 30 min; start_est = first input time minus that input's active_s; end = last input time

rules.busy: consecutive events < 3 min apart are merged ('active_s'); a longer gap is also merged when the agent is provably blocked: a foreground tool call is in flight ('tool_wait_s', e.g. a blocking until-loop waiting on a card run), the model call is in flight inside an open turn ('model_wait_s'), or the gap ends at a compaction ('compaction_s'); any other gap >= 3 min is idle (e.g. waiting for background agents/workflows or for the human). A gap in which the only calls in flight are loops watching the agent's own workflows or subagents ('watch_waits') is idle too: the subagents' hours count that time. 'tool_wait_lab_s' is the part of tool_wait_s with a card run or lab-machine command in flight. Intervals with no assistant message are dropped. Strict 3-minute-rule busy time = sum of active_s.
rules.strict: events merged into one busy interval when consecutive timestamps are < 3 min apart
rules.tool_class: watch: a Bash command matching /subagents/workflows/|/subagents/[\w-]+\.jsonl|journal\.jsonl|scratchpad/(audit|validate2)\b and not the lab pattern; lab: matching aifoundry[123]|pgrep|ettelem|claims-v3|run_\w+\.(sh|py)|horace|ablation|enercat|reruns|/done\b|run\.log|_host\b|_launcher\b|it_test|smokes; other: the rest

conc.note: value i covers minute [start + i min, +60 s); an agent counts once per minute if any busy interval overlaps it; wf = workflow agents, tool = Agent-tool agents and forks (both counting every agent); okwf, oktool = the same without the agents that failed or ended on an error, fail = those (okwf + oktool + fail = wf + tool)

rules.held: union of a card's intervals, bridging gaps under 2 min (a queue keeps the card between passes)
rules.busy: exact union of the intervals, no bridging
sources: claims-v3 host logs: "<exp> p<N> begins ... ends/failed" lines (lab-local time = PDT)
claims-v3 raw block.json t0_ms/t1_ms (cross-check; fills passes with no log line)
earlier data: first/last timestamp (t_ms, t_start_ms, t_end_ms) of every telemetry/runs/starts/marks/sweep file, merged per card and experiment when < 2 min apart
03-experiments.md stated times (cross-check; the only source for E18 and E21, flagged approx)
rules.dev: Streams the main agent's transcript line by line and keeps each foreground Bash call whose command runs a program on a card, as the first word of one of its commands: a host program (..._host, ..._launcher), the runtime's it_test, the management service's -m/-n/-t queries, ettelem sampling, a run_*.py / run_*.sh measurement script or a make with DEVICE=silicon (a program named through a shell variable set in the same command, D=...; $D, counts as its value). A call's span is its tool_use to its tool_result, so it includes any build or copy in the same command: an upper bound on the time the card was in use. The card is the machine the command ran on: aifoundry2 when local (the session's machine), else the lab machine the command was sent to; on aifoundry1 the card is ET_DEVICES or the claims-v3 scripts' V3_DEVICE (card 0 when neither is set). Excluded: simulator runs, --help, dry runs (V3_DRY=1), the text of heredocs that only write a script, quoted arguments with no space in them (a grep pattern before a script's name), and background calls (their card time is in the data files or queue logs). Subagents are left out: their card work went through the logged claims-v3 queues (agents that only write code may not reach a card), and their commands that match are analysis scripts named run_* re-run from raw data. Writes card_calls.json to $TIMELINE_DIR: The page keeps the parts of these calls that no other interval covers on that card.
rules.note: intervals before the session started (18 September) are left out; one that began before it is cut at its start

highlights.title: The session starts
highlights.caption: Remote control on, the repository cloned, spacesheep set up; at 09:26 the first research request: fine-grained power and latency observability.

highlights.title: The first card use
highlights.caption: At 09:20 a code-loading test and hello world on aifoundry2; the first memory measurements at 09:34; E1 at 09:57, one memory access taken apart by stage and power rail. The first report, Anatomy of a memory access, went out at 10:11.

highlights.title: 179 agents and a usage limit
highlights.caption: The limits-of-observability workflow started 179 agents, 10 to 15 at a time. At 10:33, as the weekly usage limit hit, the count jumped to 52 for one minute: 44 agents started in that minute and 50 of the 52 failed. The run resumed at 11:04, after the reset, and stopped at the session limit at 11:36: 99 of the 179 starts failed. The hub went live at 12:55.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: The Horace experiment
highlights.caption: A blog post’s random-matrix power experiment reproduced on the chip, rerun at one start temperature and then with strict control; from 08:44 on 21 Sep runs of up to 10 minutes were allowed. 7.7 card-hours.

highlights.title: A second card
highlights.caption: aifoundry3 joins at 12:05 with checks of its clock governor; at 12:12 E20 repeats the strict protocol on it. The DVFS brief went out at 11:51; One hot line stops a shire (13:27) and the on-chip relay page (16:02) followed that afternoon.

highlights.caption: A hierarchical catalogue of what each operation costs: first edition 08:17, every instruction on two cards by 11:28, confidence bars from reruns and cards by 13:50. 7.1 card-hours.

highlights.title: Heat per millimetre

highlights.title: The report review
highlights.caption: An audit, a fix pass and two more fix rounds, 108 workflow agents in all (up to 20 at once); 18 pages redeployed at 20:41 and again at 20:43.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: Validation overnight
highlights.caption: Every analysis re-run from raw data, then PLAN2: a shared chart toolkit, data regenerated and interactive charts, 108 workflow agents through the night; 18 pages redeployed at 07:18.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: Claims check v3 begins
highlights.caption: Version 3 of the claims check, pre-registered at 09:08; its first passes ran on aifoundry2 and aifoundry3 from 10:01 (11.8 card-hours before the machine fixes, kept as a separate set).
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: aifoundry1 fixed
highlights.caption: The broken lab machine troubleshot read-only from 12:56, a report at 14:16; fixed and its fix log published at 15:05, made public at 15:12.

highlights.title: The v3 campaign on three cards
highlights.caption: 17:23 on 25 Sep to 06:53 on 26 Sep: aifoundry2, aifoundry3 and aifoundry1 card 1 through the night, 34.2 card-hours of pre-registered passes.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: Four cards, then three
highlights.caption: aifoundry1’s two cards join at 17:12 (amendment A2). All four cards were in use at once for 4 minutes in all (17:28, 17:41, 17:45 and 17:56), in smoke tests and a temperature check of card 0; at 17:56 card 0 was excluded because it overheats under load (A4).

highlights.title: The crash root cause
highlights.caption: aifoundry3’s host crashes traced to a log-level race in the runtime, reproduced without a card (E49) and fixed at 23:15. At 06:16 on 26 Sep, 641 host processes of the fixed build ran on the card without a crash.

highlights.title: The visualization pass
highlights.caption: 8 agents and 6 forks survey the pages and add interactive charts (a card selector, calculators, a claim scoreboard); 19 pages redeployed at 00:08.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: Gathers and scatters (E48)
highlights.caption: Queued behind the campaign on three cards, 03:19 to 09:22 on 26 Sep: 3.6 card-hours.

highlights.title: The three-card page updates
highlights.caption: 15 agents and 12 forks fold the campaign’s results into every page; ten commits at 08:37 on the pages branch.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: The weekly limit
highlights.caption: At 08:41 on 26 Sep the account reached its weekly usage limit, and this session’s agents paused until it reset at 11:00 on 27 Sep. The cards finished their queues by 09:22, and another Claude session made 21 commits that evening, 16:00 to 23:26.

highlights.title: Chip diagram and this timeline
highlights.caption: The owner asks for an interactive chip diagram for a talk, this timeline and experiments on heat placement; 4 workflows start by 11:17.

highlights.title: The chip diagram and the PCIe link
highlights.caption: An animated chip schematic for the talk went out at 13:39. The owner’s feedback at 14:08 asked, among other things, to measure the PCIe link it called “not measured”: E50 measured it on three cards, 14:24 to 15:13 (15 runs of about 14 s), and its page went out at 18:09 with the diagram’s second version (commit 18:10).
links: The PCIe link and the launch path

highlights.title: Heat placement
highlights.caption: Does the thermal throttle follow the mean of the die’s sensors or one hot shire, and does the same work placed at the die’s edges run longer before it? Designed, critiqued and pre-registered by 3 workflows; the owner’s decisions at 12:49. Development on aifoundry3 from 16:52 to 22:10, then aifoundry1 card 1 from 20:24, its validation passes from 23:45 to 07:49; aifoundry2 ran 2 short sessions, the first at 16:50. 4.5 card-hours in all.
links: Where the work sits: placement and the thermal trip

highlights.title: The chip diagram polished
highlights.caption: At 20:15 the owner asks for a more professional walkthrough and zoom, then another pass over the pages: 8 agents polish the diagram (motion, a visual system, the tour; commit 23:52) while 9 agents add charts and fix correctness across the observability pages (commit 21:51). At 22:24 the zoom still jumps; 3 agents trace it to the page’s own drawing, and the smooth zoom goes out at 00:20.

highlights.title: DV2: the governor and heat
highlights.caption: At 21:47 the owner asks for another set of DVFS and heat experiments. Theories, a design and its critique came before any card work; the development night on aifoundry2 ran 00:39 to 02:54: 21 read-only watch cycles, 3 sessions and 1 smoke launch, 1.0 card-hours. Development only: the validation plan was frozen afterwards; its queue started at 20:45 on Mon 28 Sep (the last highlight).
links: The DVFS loop and its leakage

highlights.title: aifoundry2 hangs
highlights.caption: In the DV2 session that began at 02:50, aifoundry2’s Master Minion stopped taking work: the second launch never started its kernel, and the next could not reach the command queue. The queue stopped at 02:54. No reset was attempted then, by the lab’s rules; the card came back at 08:32, after the owner approved a reset (below).
links: The DVFS loop and its leakage

highlights.title: Memory levels, interactively
highlights.caption: At 20:37 the owner asks for an interactive diagram of each memory level, down to the transistors, with what nobody knows added to the asks for the team. 16 agents in two workflows built them; the page went out at 05:07, with the hub and the chip diagram updated a minute later.
links: Anatomy of a memory access, interactively

highlights.title: The status, and every task at once
highlights.caption: At 06:14 the owner asks for the status and for parallel agents to finish every open task: a workflow of 22 agents runs from 06:16 to 08:37 (the heat report and its verdicts, a sweep of the review’s open items, an earlier refresh of this timeline, and a rebuild on aifoundry1).
links: Where the work sits: placement and the thermal trip

highlights.title: Machine fixes, and aifoundry2 back
highlights.caption: At 06:33 the owner lets the machine-level fixes that were waiting go ahead: 10 agents export aifoundry3’s system log and raise its size cap, install the new card-holder and health-check tools on the three machines, free 2.4 GB on aifoundry1 and stop orphaned browsers. The owner approves resetting the hung card at 06:35: the per-card sysfs reset re-attaches it but the Master Minion stays hung; after a second approval at 08:32 the management reset brings it back at 08:32, and a test kernel runs cleanly. At 06:39 the owner asks that the requests for the lab lead keep only what needs the team (5 agents).

highlights.title: Heat placement: the verdicts
highlights.caption: The validation on aifoundry1 card 1 ends at 07:49: 10 blocks, all valid. Short bursts pass (the same work on the perimeter took 2.04 times as long to heat the die as in the interior, 5 of 5 blocks); the primary sustained test is inconclusive (7 of its 10 runs met the 150 s cap), so under the frozen rules no theory survived and none was refuted. The report goes out at 09:07.
links: Where the work sits: placement and the thermal trip

highlights.title: The effect of overheating
highlights.caption: At 08:41 the owner asks what temperatures processors are built for, whether a limit should watch the average or the hottest spot, what heat does to switching speed, and why a hot chip stops and then recovers. 11 agents research it (69 sources, 60 of them outside), test it and write it up; E53 ran on aifoundry3 and aifoundry1 card 1 from 10:11 to 12:04 (3.2 card-hours): the hottest sensor ran 1–3 °C above the mean, and 663 checked launches up to an 81 °C mean computed nothing wrong. The page goes out at 13:41.

highlights.title: The walkthrough on phones
highlights.caption: At 09:07 the owner reports the chip diagram cut off on a phone. 4 agents find the cause in the page itself (a minimum width, and a scroll to the middle of the canvas), not in the host; the phone layout, the whole die in the width, goes out at 12:04, and the host’s comment tab over the page’s left edge is reported to its team.
links: Anatomy of a memory access, interactively

highlights.title: The timeline refreshed
highlights.caption: At 13:55 the owner asks to bring this timeline up to date with the latest experiments; the refresh goes out at 14:08, and again at 14:29 and 14:38 after the owner’s two notes on it (14:23: lead each message with what it asked, the timing in small print; 14:35: link the pages each highlight produced).

highlights.title: Requests from the pages themselves
highlights.caption: At 14:10 the owner has the session listen for messages written on the published pages, in their Talk tab: 5 arrive by the snapshot. The memory levels get light tints instead of dotted and striped backgrounds (commit 14:22); the chip diagram gets an eleventh data flow, B, Broadcast (Q62, asked at 14:51, live at 15:59); one message is feedback meant for the spacesheep team.
links: Anatomy of a memory access, interactively

highlights.title: The superseded energies folded in
highlights.caption: At 16:00 the owner points out the sections still marked “energies superseded”. 3 agents fold the newer energies into the memory anatomy, memory hierarchy, on-chip communication and matmul pages (commit 16:45), then sparse compute’s power from three cards and the first pass’s leftovers (commit 17:33); 11 pages go out at 17:36.

highlights.title: Heat per mm: the 2× gap (Q63)
highlights.caption: At 16:09 the owner asks, from the heat-per-mm page, which process node the cited wire-energy figure is for and whether a 2× gap between it and the measurement is expected. 12 agents and forks read the figure’s papers, talks and interviews and the NoC energies measured on other chips; the answer is committed at 17:29 and live at 17:32. At 18:38 the owner asks for a light cyan background: live at 18:39.

highlights.title: A major pass, and this timeline in the repository
highlights.caption: At 20:41 the owner asks for a major pass now that the lab works again: every remaining lab fix and check, the NoC validation, the to-do list, and this timeline committed to the repository. At 20:51 four of the lab report’s host fixes go in on aifoundry1, owner-approved (among them a headless default and unused desktop services turned off); the rest, on all three machines, wait for the owner, since the session’s permission check refused them. A workflow of 8 agents studies the NoC’s voltage control, a wire benchmark, a lab-wide audit and the lab tools, then designs the NoC-voltage experiment and its runner; another of 4 moves this page and its tools into the repository, with a privacy scan of its data (commit 21:52, live at 21:52).

highlights.title: DV2 validation: three sessions
highlights.caption: The DV2 validation on aifoundry2 has run under its frozen plan since 20:45 on 28 Sep: a read-only temperature reading every 3 minutes (86 by the snapshot; the idle card read 73–75 °C at night), and a heating session only when the card is cool enough. 3 replication sessions ran, 22:13–22:30, 22:42–23:06 and 23:19–23:56, each starting at 59–60 °C, with 1, 2 and 4 complete test blocks (the queue log); the Master Minion, which hung on the development night, kept taking work. The readings go on until about 16:45 on 29 Sep; the reduction comes after.
links: The DVFS loop and its leakage

highlights.title: NV: the NoC validation, frozen and waiting
highlights.caption: The NoC validation the owner asked for (E54): does the mesh’s energy per bit·mm follow its 0.485 V supply, as heat per mm’s answer to Q63 assumed? A read-only probe of aifoundry3 at 22:54 finds the NoC rail at 485 mV and 400 MHz; at 23:06 the predictions are frozen and the experiment registered, before any card write. The first voltage write, 540 then 600 mV and back, did not start: the session’s permission check refused a command that changes a shared card’s state, so it waits for the owner. The validation is planned on aifoundry2 after DV2.

highlights.title: Four experiments, developed and validated
highlights.caption: 12 agents build and pre-register four experiments on the hub’s open questions (commit 23:47). Each is developed on aifoundry1 card 1 (23:47–00:53), frozen, then validated on aifoundry3 (00:04–01:06), 0.9 card-hours in all. E55: two host-to-card copies in flight in one stream move 0.49 of what one moves at 64 MB, while one in each of two streams loses nothing, and a host write lands in the L3. E56: read replies go y first and write requests x first on both cards, where the chip diagram assumed x first for every route; a link saturates near 92 GB/s. E57: the DRAM bank and row map and per-controller refresh hold on aifoundry3, the L2 keeps TensorLoad lines, and stride-256 runs at 0.665 of the bandwidth; no theory of the 128 B per cycle cap survives. E58: the rails’ meters filter with a time constant of 1.01–1.06 s on every rail of aifoundry3 (0.54 s on card 1’s SRAM rail). The PCIe runner’s first card run since its lock fix, at 23:56, exits cleanly.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub
The PCIe link and the launch path

highlights.title: Sparse parity: research, then a build
highlights.caption: At 21:14 the owner queues the next task: a sparse-parity solver that uses the chip’s thousand cores, prototyped at toy sizes first and then scaled to the whole chip. A workflow of 5 agents (21:21–22:53, no card) surveys the literature, maps the problem onto the chip and tries CPU toys: the design finds a noisy sparse parity by exhaustive correlation, computed as int8 tensor matrix products, and its critique puts the honest gain at about 2–5× a tuned 8-core host and 5–10× less energy. From 00:47 on Tue 29 Sep a second workflow builds the CPU reference and the first kernel. The data ends at the snapshot, 02:15 on Tue 29 Sep.
